content: Postpartum constipation is a common condition that affects mothers and is characterized by symptoms such as pain or discomfort, straining during defecation, and hard stools. Several factors contribute to this condition, including hemorrhoids, pain at the site of an episiotomy, hormonal changes during pregnancy, and the use of iron supplements (haematinics) during pregnancy. To address this issue, healthcare providers often recommend dietary modifications, such as consuming a high-fiber diet and increasing fluid intake. Laxatives are also commonly used to relieve constipation, but the effectiveness and safety of these interventions for preventing postpartum constipation require further evaluation. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of various interventions aimed at preventing postpartum constipation. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared any intervention—pharmacological (e.g., laxatives) or non-pharmacological (e.g., acupuncture, educational, or behavioral interventions)—against another intervention, placebo, or no intervention in postpartum women. Trials using quasi-randomized designs or cluster-RCTs were also eligible, but no cross-over trials were included. The review included five trials involving 1,208 postpartum women. These trials consisted of three RCTs and two quasi-RCTs. Four of the trials compared a laxative with a placebo, while one trial compared a combination of a laxative and a bulking agent with the same laxative alone in women who had undergone surgical repair of third-degree perineal tears. Most of the trials were poorly reported, and four of the five trials were published over 40 years ago. The risk of bias was judged to be unclear for most domains, with a high risk of selection and attrition bias overall. In the comparison of laxatives versus placebo, four trials were included. However, two of these trials examined laxatives that are no longer in use—Danthron, which has carcinogenic properties, and Bisoxatin acetate, which is not recommended for lactating women. As a result, their findings were excluded from the main analysis. None of the trials assessed the primary outcomes of interest, such as pain or straining during defecation, the incidence of postpartum constipation, or quality of life. Secondary outcomes were also largely unreported. One trial with 471 women provided low-certainty evidence suggesting that the laxative senna may increase the number of women having their first bowel movement within 24 hours after delivery (risk ratio [RR] 2.90, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.24 to 3.75). However, very low-certainty evidence suggested that senna may have little or no effect on the number of women having their first bowel movement on the first day after delivery (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.22). Low-certainty evidence indicated that senna may reduce the number of women having their first bowel movement on the second day (RR 0.23, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.45) and the third day (RR 0.05, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.89) after delivery. Very low-certainty evidence suggested that senna may have little or no effect on the number of women having their first bowel movement on the fourth day after delivery (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.87). Adverse effects were poorly reported, but low-certainty evidence suggested that senna may increase the number of women experiencing abdominal cramps (RR 4.23, 95% CI 1.75 to 10.19). Very low-certainty evidence suggested that laxatives taken by the mother may have little or no effect on loose stools in the baby (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.16 to 2.41) or diarrhea in the baby (RR 2.46, 95% CI 0.23 to 26.82). In the comparison of a laxative plus a bulking agent versus a laxative alone, very low-certainty evidence from one trial involving 147 women suggested no significant difference between the two groups in terms of the time to the first bowel movement after delivery. The trial reported the time to the first bowel movement as a median (range) and found no evidence of a difference in the incidence of postpartum constipation, although data were not reported. Very low-certainty evidence suggested that the combination of a laxative and a bulking agent may increase the number of women experiencing any episode of fecal incontinence during the first 10 days postpartum (RR 1.81, 95% CI 1.01 to 3.23). The trial did not report on adverse effects of the intervention on babies or many of the secondary outcomes. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to draw general conclusions about the effectiveness and safety of laxatives for preventing postpartum constipation. The evidence was assessed as being of low to very low certainty due to limitations in study design, indirectness, and imprecision. No trials were identified that assessed educational or behavioral interventions. Further rigorous trials are needed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of laxatives during the postpartum period. Future studies should also investigate educational and behavioral interventions, as well as positions that may enhance defecation. These trials should report on primary outcomes such as pain or straining during defecation, the incidence of postpartum constipation, quality of life, time to the first bowel movement after delivery, and adverse effects of the interventions, including nausea, vomiting, pain, and flatulence.
